newsitem.title: UK: British scientists picture how galaxies form.
newsitem.headline: British scientists picture how galaxies form.

text.p: British astronomers said on Tuesday they were starting to form a picture of how galaxies were formed, thanks to stunning new observations by the orbiting Hubble Space Telescope and other equipment.

Early galaxies were created by matter forming into clumps and pulling in gas, gradually growing into spiral shapes and then into ellipses, Carlos Frenk of Durham University and colleagues told astronomers at the National Astronomer Meeting in Southampton.

Deep, hard looks at the very edges of the universe have revealed "baby" galaxies only a billion years old -- one-tenth of the minimum age of the universe today. Because of the huge distances involved, astronomers are essentially looking backwards in time.
In September astronomers using Hubble said they had identified "blobs" in which they believed were the basic building blocks of galaxies.
The 18 blobs were behind the constellation Hercules, 11 billion light-years away (a light-year is the distance light travels in a year at 300,000 km or 186,000 miles a second).
In June another team of scientists reported they had seen the birth of what would have been the first stars. Frenk said his team was starting to put this information together.

"It is rather like having a snapshot of different individuals at selected stages of development -- say a baby, an infant, a young teenager and an old man -- and then trying to piece together a picture of genetic evolution from this information," he said.

"Clearly, this is only possible if one has an understanding of the basic biological processes at work," Frenk said, adding that astronomers and cosmologists were now beginning to gain this understanding.
Frenk's group fit the observations into a computer simulation, and have been able to create a picture of how galaxies evolved.
Frenk first reported on his computer programme a year ago, and said it showed an almost Biblical start to the universe, with order taking over from chaos.

He told this week's meeting that the simulations continue to fit in with a 1992 discovery of "ripples" in space made using the U.S. National Aeronautics and Space Administration's COBE satellite. The ripples were hailed as the "discovery of the century" by physicists.
Big Bang theory says the universe was formed in a split second 10 to 15 billion years ago from a tiny pinpoint.
Hot gas cooled down into matter, which gravity pulled into stars and planets, but for that to happen there must have been slight irregularities -- the ripples.
If matter had been spread evenly, there would have been no reason for anything to fall one way or another and no structures -- no galaxies, stars or planets -- would have formed.
